headline: Punjab is the new hub of cancer care. 2 Tata Memorial hospitals are making all the difference
content: In the dusty village of Dhaipai in Punjab’s Malwa region, where tractors keep pace with cars, Gursewak Singh, 40, lives with his wife and children as caretakers in the home of a family who has migrated to Australia. A much-in-demand plumber in the nearby Bhikhi town, Gursewak worked and occasionally entertained friends by singing aloud. Life was good. His daughter had just topped her Class 12 commerce class and was on her way to college; his son was keen on studying computer science. “My work kept me busy. At times, I would make Rs 5,000 a day,” he says. Then, in August 2024, his stomach began to distend. He did not think of it much until one day, he woke up with excruciating pain. His family first took him some 20 km away to the district hospital in Mansa. He was then taken to AIIMS Bathinda, which referred him to the Homi Bhabha Cancer Hospital in Sangrur. There, a bone marrow test detected cancerous cells. “I was told to go to the hospital’s Mullanpur branch for a PET scan and other tests for which the hospital in Sangrur did not have facilities at the time,” says Gursewak. When he reached Mullanpur, in New Chandigarh, Gursewak was struck by the hospital building. “It was a very expensive, modern facility,” he recalls. After tests confirmed that he had hairy cell leukaemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow, Dr Pooja Prasad of the Department of Medical Oncology examined him. “She said I would have to be admitted for a fortnight,” says Gursewak, who recalls feeling overwhelmed by the diagnosis and worries over treatment costs. “No one in my family has had cancer.” Without another word, he left the hospital. Back in his village, a friend suggested he start treatment at a government facility in Faridkot. Gursewak even began chemotherapy. “But I had a terrible reaction and felt like I would die,” he says. In early 2025, he returned to Mullanpur. “I told the doctor I cannot afford expensive treatment. She said that at this hospital, no one gets turned away for want of funds,” he says. For long, Punjab’s Malwa region, which includes the cotton belt in Sri Muktsar Sahib, Mansa, Faridkot and Bathinda districts, has borne the state’s cancer burden. Over time, the numbers in Doaba and Majha, the other two regions, caught up too. According to the National Cancer Registry Programme, the state recorded 43,196 cancer cases in 2025, up from 39,521 in 2021. Until a decade ago, people from across Punjab boarded what came to be known as the “cancer train” to Rajasthan, where the Acharya Tulsi Regional Cancer Treatment and Research Institute in Bikaner offered subsidised treatments. Starting from Abohar and stopping at Bathinda at 9 pm, the overnight train carried scores of patients to Bikaner. The train, and the painful journeys many undertook, symbolised all that was wrong with public healthcare in the state. Many of them boarded the train because they had nowhere else to go. But today, the Homi Bhabha Cancer Hospital in Sangrur and its main campus in New Chandigarh (Mullanpur) have managed to change the way the region accesses cancer care. The Sangrur and Mullanpur facilities are part of a network of cancer treatment and research facilities operated by the Tata Memorial Centre under the Central government’s Department of Atomic Energy. Set up with a goal to decentralise cancer care and bring the services of the Mumbai-headquartered Tata Memorial Centre directly to North India, the two public hospitals have drawn patients not only from Punjab but Haryana and Rajasthan too. The hospitals have also helped to take some of the burden off Chandigarh’s Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education & Research (PGIMER), whose oncology departments see around 300 patients daily. “Everyone was scared of the cancer train. It was commonly believed that those who boarded it never returned,” says Kulwinder Singh, who is visiting the Sangrur facility from Sardulgarh, near Bathinda, with his mother, who has been diagnosed with cancer. The number of patients taking the ‘cancer train’ has dropped sharply after 2015, when the Sangrur hospital opened its doors. It dropped further after the Mullanpur centre started operating in 2022. Hospital records demonstrate this: Punjab’s share among patients arriving at the Bikaner facility’s OPD from outside Rajasthan fell from 27% in 2015 to 9% in 2020. According to estimates by senior officials at the Bikaner facility, the daily inflow of patients from Punjab has fallen — from about 100 several years ago to about five. “The train journey has been reversed,” says Dr Tapas Kumar Dora, the first oncologist to arrive at the Sangrur hospital when it opened in 2015 and is now its officer in charge. This year, by September 30, the Sangrur hospital had logged 5,751 new cancer patients and Mullanpur 10,059, bringing the total to 15,810 — just short of the 16,035 new patients recorded by the two campuses in 2025. Roughly 50% of the patients at Mullanpur are from Punjab, while people from Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir and Uttar Pradesh make up the rest. At Sangrur, 90% of the patients are from Punjab. These numbers show two things, says Dr Ashish Gulia, the director under whom both the Sangrur and Mullanpur centres operate. “They show the cancer burden in the region. But they also show growing trust,” he says. Manjit Kaur is at the Sangrur hospital with her husband Gurmail Singh, 69, who is recovering from a surgery to remove a cancerous cyst in his gums. From Uchhi Rabbon near Malerkotla, where the couple has three milch cattle and just enough to meet their expenses, they used the Ayushman Bharat scheme to fund the surgery. “We chose this hospital because it is where five villagers from Uchhi Rabbon were cured of cancer,” says Manjit. For Gurmail, it has already been a month at the hospital. Manjit spends her days by his bed in a 20-patient ward. Her nights are spent in the dharamshala on campus that’s free for patient attendants. Free langar served on the premises covers her meals. For Gurmail’s after-care, doctors have now advised them to stay on for another week. Under the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY), eligible families receive up to Rs 5 lakh a year for cancer treatment and hospitalisation at empanelled facilities, but routine outpatient visits and extended stays are excluded. Dr Gulia says that almost 85% of patients across the Sangrur and Mullanpur facilities receive free or heavily subsidised treatment through one of the many government schemes — Ayushman Bharat, Punjab’s Mukh Mantri Sehat Yojana, Himachal Pradesh’s HIMCARE, the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme (ECHS) or the Employees’ State Insurance Scheme (ESI). For those outside these schemes, the hospital draws on donor-funded pools, including a patient welfare fund and a fund for scans or biopsies, which also covers patients before they can avail of the Ayushman Bharat funds. “Last year, we generated more than Rs 60 crore,” Gulia says. “If anybody is curable, that person should not suffer.” Dr Gulia says their larger ambition is to control cost. “A robotic surgery here can be done with just Rs 75,000, compared to Rs 2.5-3 lakh at a corporate hospital. We remove the middleman,” he says. Under the Tata Memorial network, medicines for all patients are centrally procured at discounts, directly from companies, after tendering. The average savings come to 40-50% below the maximum retail price, says Dr Gulia. Manjit is now being guided by the hospital’s ‘kevat’ service on schemes that can help fund their additional stay. Named after the boatmen who ferried Lord Rama across the Sarayu, the kevats serve as patient guides, helping them navigate complex financial, administrative and medical challenges. Sometimes, they connect patients with others facing similar struggles. At the hospital in Sangrur, Satinder Kaur, her head wrapped in a black scarf, rests after her latest round of chemotherapy. Since she was diagnosed with Stage 2 breast cancer six months ago, she has been taking the bus from her village, Moonak, to Sangrur for her doctor visits. Her doctors, she says, have assured her that the chemotherapy will cure her. “It’s not fatal so long as it’s detected on time,” she says. Sangrur was not the first choice for Punjab’s first Tata Memorial Hospital. In 2013, then Punjab Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal, who wanted to set up a cancer-care facility in the state, led a delegation of officials to Mumbai to meet then Tata Memorial Hospital director Dr R A Badwe. The Tata Memorial Centre was interested in a facility in Chandigarh or Mohali, and land was accordingly allotted in Mullanpur, in the northern part of Mohali. However, rural Punjab urgently needed cancer care, and the project at Mullanpur was expected to take years. Then Sangrur MP Vijay Inder Singla sought the intervention of then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, finally paving the way for the facility in Sangrur, adjacent to the Civil Hospital. On a foggy January day in 2015, Dr Tapas arrived in Sangrur, transferred from the Tata Memorial Centre in Mumbai. With the help of Lakhbir Singh, a local ITI graduate who doubled up as an electrical and civil engineer, he immediately got to work. “We innovated and improvised every day,” says Dr Tapas, who hails from Odisha and completed his MBBS and MD (Radiation Oncology) degrees from Cuttack. Showing old photos of workers building the aerial bridge that now connects the hospital’s new and old buildings, Dr Tapas recalls that locals would line up to see what was coming up. By March 2015, the operation theatre had been set up in what was a store in the Civil Hospital. With patients starting to trickle in, the cancer facility began operating with just six beds. In 2016, Dr Tapas commissioned a linear accelerator for treating tumours with targeted radiation, followed by a bronchoscope to check for lung cancer in 2018. Interventional radiology was introduced in the hospital in 2021. But there were other problems. Few trained doctors wanted to come to Sangrur from Mumbai. Initially, they got new residents to serve a one-year bond. “Some ended up liking it here and stayed on,” says Dr Tapas. Next, they started a few paramedical courses, for which students with Punjab domicile were given preference. After they graduated, they had to work at the hospital for at least a year, a strategy that ensured a steady stream of paramedical staff. Currently, the Sangrur facility has 240 students in six courses, including BSc Medical Radiography and Imaging Technology, BSc Radiotherapy Technology and BSc Operation Theatre Technology. The hospital has now expanded to 150 beds and four OTs. Currently, its outpatient footfall is nearly 250 patients daily, and bed occupancy is over 90%. The centre has two external beam machines that treat nearly 100 patients daily. It also provides patients with CT scans, MRI, digital X-ray, ultrasonography, mammography, and nuclear medicine services. Its dedicated cancer prevention department holds cancer screening camps in villages across Punjab, and cancer walkathons and seminars in government schools in the state. Dr Tapas says relocating to Sangrur was “the best decision” of his life. “The patients are grateful and are always showering blessings on the staff. This is very different from my experience elsewhere,” he says. The first thing anyone notices at the Mullanpur facility is not the queue, the smell of disinfectant or the anxiety that usually hangs over a cancer ward. It’s the light that streams into the waiting hall from the cathedral-like ceiling. The corridors are wide and spotless. There is air, space and an unusual calm. The building was designed, its director says, to make people feel less afraid. “Cancer is curable. But the fear delays people,” says Dr Gulia. “We wanted a hospital where a patient does not feel trapped.” On August 24, 2022, Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Mullanpur centre. While land had been allocated in 2012-13, the project had remained stuck due to issues with environment clearance, land acquisition, finances and then Covid-19. “It was a pretty tough journey,” says Dr Gulia, who moved to Punjab from Mumbai’s Tata Memorial Centre in 2023. “But within a year and a half of operation, we were almost fully occupied.” The hospital has 300-320 beds, 14 operation theatres and two radiotherapy machines. It has a bone marrow transplant unit, and offers robotic surgery and CAR-T cell therapy. Dr Gulia says barring proton therapy, which involves a Rs 600-crore machine, the Mullanpur centre has “every other world-class facility”. For now, patients who need the therapy are referred to Tata Memorial’s Mumbai facility. Across the Sangrur and Mullanpur hospitals, there are more than 200 doctors, 500 nursing staff, 300 support staff and 700 administrative staff. Specialists and staff move between the campuses, allowing patients to draw on a wider pool of expertise. Dr Gulia, who is based in Mullanpur but visits Sangrur with his team every week, estimates that the two centres have treated nearly a lakh patients so far. He expects nearly 20,000 new patients this year, since “the burden of common cancers shows no sign of diminishing”. It was at the Mullanpur centre that Gursewak, the plumber from Dhaipai village who was diagnosed with hairy cell leukaemia, spent six months starting January 2025. His wife, Sandeep Kaur, 39, stayed at the on-campus dharamshala, sometimes sleeping on a mattress next to his bed. “We did not have to pay a paisa for the chemotherapy or the medicines. We only spent on tea for relatives who occasionally came to see me,” he says. He has been cancer-free for over a year and currently does not need any medication. “I simply eat healthy and walk 8 km a day,” he says Gursewak, who is now back at work. Once in a while, he boards a bus that leaves for Chandigarh at 5.30 am, and reaches Mullanpur in just three hours. At the hospital, he meets patients and tells them to hold on. “I tell them to be mentally strong. You have to first beat it in your dimaag (mind),” says the 40-year-old.

headline: UNA assures long-term commitment to Jos route, plans more destinations
content: UNITED Nigeria Airlines (UNA) has assured passengers in Plateau of its long-term commitment to the Lagos to Jos route. The airline dismissed concerns that the new service to General Yakubu Gowon International Airport, Jos, might be a seasonal operation introduced to take advantage of the Christmas travel period. The airline’s Managing Director, Mr Osita Okonkwo, gave the assurance during the inaugural flight ceremony in Jos on Tuesday. Okoknkwo said that the decision to start operations to the Jos was driven by the route’s commercial prospects and its potential to connect different parts of the country. ‘’The airline is committed to developing new routes and sustaining operations once our commercial viability has been established. “You know, if you have followed United Nigeria Airlines for the last six years, we do not start and stop. It takes us time to start, but once we start, we continue,” he said. He described Jos as an important destination because of Plateau’s central location, which provides opportunities to connect travellers from the southern and Eastern parts of the country to the North. According to him, the state’s growing focus on tourism and investment also makes the route commercially attractive. He noted that the current improved air connectivity drive would make it easier for business people, investors and tourists to access the state. He said that the airline would initially operate two-weekly flights to Jos on Tuesdays and Fridays. He added that the frequency could increase to three, four or daily services depending on passenger demand. Okonkwo also disclosed that the airline was considering additional domestic destinations, including Yola and Maiduguri, as part of its ongoing fleet and route expansion programme. He added that the airline was also working toward regional and international expansion, with investments in aircraft, personnel and commercial partnerships. The Plateau Governor, Mr Caleb Mutfwang, pledged the state’s support for the airline, describing the new route as an important development for tourism, investment and economic growth. Mutfwang was represented by the Speaker, Plateau House of Assembly, Mr Daniel Naanlong. The governor welcomed the airline, stating that improved air connectivity was essential to achieving the state’s tourism ambitions. He noted that the government was working to restore major hospitality facilities, including Plateau Hotel and Hill Station Hotel. He assured the airline of the state’s support in security, partnership and efforts to encourage residents to patronise its services. Also, the state Commissioner for Transportation, Mr Jatau Gyang, said that the new connection was part of the government’s broader efforts to link the state with other regions. He said that the development would reduce the difficulties faced by residents traveling to the South-East and South-South. He explained that the proposed Jos to Owerri connection would provide easier access to several states in the two regions. Gyang added that this would reduce the need for passengers to travel through Abuja or Lagos to reach their destinations. Gyang also highlighted ongoing efforts to improve tourism infrastructure, including the Jos Wildlife Park, Hill Station Hotel and Plateau Hotel. He added that the government was considering the rehabilitation of Assop Falls. He further disclosed that the state government was working toward establishing its own airline, Air Plateau, as part of efforts to strengthen aviation development and connectivity. The Airport Manager, Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN), Mrs Chidinma Ekpo said that the new route would promote tourism, facilitate business activities and stimulate economic growth. She said: “We remain dedicated to working with all relevant stakeholders to ensure sustainability of this operation. Let people to Plateau state take advantage of this opportunity.’’ A passenger aboard the inaugural flight, Dr Panam Percy-Paul, applauded the airline and the government of Plateau, saying that he had a smooth flight. An airport staff, who pleaded anonymity, expressed excitement with the development, saying, ‘’Plateau residents will no longer be stranded.’’ The flight was greeted with a water cannon salute, cultural displays and received by the Igbo Community in Jos. headline: Who pays for climate change is a federal question
content: In the 1990s, several U.S. States sued the tobacco companies to hold them accountable for the health hazards of cigarettes. This litigation led to a 1998 Master Settlement Agreement, under which the companies committed at least $206 billion over 25 years as compensation for the harmful effects of cigarettes. Inspired by the famous tobacco litigation case of the 1990s, a small county called Boulder in Colorado, U.S., initiated a major litigation under the State law, in 2018, to fix liability on major oil and gas companies for the impact of climate change. The suit claimed compensation for recovering the costs of coping with wildfires, floods and heat by building a case on public nuisance and consumer protection. In May 2025, the Colorado Supreme Court allowed the suit to proceed, holding that federal law did not pre-empt Boulder’s claims for damages under State law. The oil companies, now backed by the Donald Trump administration, argue that federal law, including the Clean Air Act and the very structure of the American Constitution, forbids a State from applying its own law to global emissions. They argue that a State cannot use its own tort law to make companies pay for harm from global emissions. This case has now ended up in the U.S. Supreme Court which recently heard arguments on the most important question in climate governance: who pays for climate disasters, and whether States have a role in formulating climate policy? The Indian nexus Since climate change is an international phenomenon, the issue in the U.S. has a direct nexus with India. When climate disasters affect India, its States are left to its own devices, with little help from any direction. When landslides tore through Mundakkai and Chooralmala in Wayanad on July 30, 2024, the Keralam government reported 298 deaths and 32 missing people. The Union took nearly five months to declare the tragedy a “disaster of severe nature”, and when assistance for rehabilitation came, it came not as a grant but as a 50-year interest-free loan of ₹529.50 crore. After the 2023 floods in Himachal Pradesh, the State government pegged the losses at ₹9,042 crore. Even though the Union Government released ₹633.73 crore in NDRF assistance for immediate relief, it sanctioned only a meagre ₹2,006.40 crore for recovery and reconstruction plan nearly two years after the disaster. In Punjab, after the floods of August and September 2025, the State government demanded ₹20,000 crore in immediate relief. The Union government announced only ₹1,600 crore as the relief. Like in Boulder, the governments that bear the costs of climate disasters are not the ones that control the climate policy. The Union occupies the field The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 were enacted by Parliament to give effect to the Stockholm Conference of 1972. Article 253, under which the Air Act and Water Act were enacted, permits Parliament to legislate on any subject, including those in the State List, to implement an international agreement. Once climate change is framed as a treaty obligation, the Union can claim the entire field. The law on disaster management deepens the imbalance. ‘Disaster’ finds no mention in any of the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule; Parliament enacted the Disaster Management Act, 2005 by drawing on entries in the Concurrent List such as ‘social security and social insurance’, the participation of the States in the framing of environment policy is minimal. The Union has also kept the revenue that climate policy generates. The Clean Environment Cess on coal, raised to ₹400 a tonne in 2016, which was collected entirely by the Union, since Article 270(1) keeps cesses outside the pool of taxes shared with the States. Can the States claim the Clean Environment Cess for climate relief? In M.K. Ranjitsinh vs Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court of India recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21, observing that the absence of a single climate statute “does not mean that the people of India do not have a right against the adverse effects of climate change”. Earlier, M.C. Mehta vs Union of India (1987) laid down the rule of absolute liability for hazardous industries, and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum vs Union of India (1996) made the “polluter pays” principle part of the law of the land. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 empowers the tribunal to award compensation for environmental damage. But despite the spread of law across different statutes, real polluters have rarely paid for polluting the environment in India. The Sikkim High Court has now opened a door that the law has so far left shut. In September 2026, a Bench led by Chief Justice A. Muhamed Mustaque initiated a suo motu public interest litigation, In Re: Climatic Justice in the State of Sikkim, after the flash floods in neighbouring Nepal. The Court has called for climate-risk assessments from the State’s departments and all six districts. The Bench has also called for a shift from “reactive disaster management” to an “anticipatory and participatory model of climate governance”. For a Himalayan State that saw the glacial lake outburst flood in the Teesta valley in October 2023, the case gives the Court a chance to confront the question that federalism has so far avoided: when a State suffers a climate disaster, who must bear its cost, and what does the Union owe it? Sharing the financial burden We are confronting a climate crisis and the need of the hour is a decentralised system in climate governance. Our climate change policy is deeply centralised which takes away the States power to act without giving them the means to recover. The way forward lies in sharing both the authority and the burden. The Finance Commission may have to start considering climate vulnerability as a criterion in the devolution of funds. Disaster relief to the States must come as grants, not as loans with deadlines attached, and within a fixed time after a disaster. Levies on fossil fuels must be shared with the States that bear their costs. The U.S. Supreme Court will decide who may sue for climate damage and against whom. India must decide, before the next major disaster, who pays for it. Mukund P. Unny is an Advocate-on-Record at the Supreme Court of India.

headline: SC Collegium recommends new Chief Justices for Karnataka, Jharkhand, Tripura HCs
content: New Delhi: The Supreme Court Collegium, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, on Monday recommended new Chief Justices for the High Courts of Jharkhand, Karnataka and Tripura. Justice Vibhu Bakhru, currently Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court, has been recommended for transfer as Chief Justice of the Jharkhand High Court. Justice M S Ramachandra Rao, Chief Justice of the Tripura High Court, has been recommended to take over as Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court. The move will fill the vacancy arising on November 27, when the incumbent retires. Bakhru was elevated to the Delhi High Court in 2013 and served there for over a decade before his appointment as Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court in 2025. .CJI Surya Kant recuses himself from hearing plea related to Supertech projects.He has now been recommended to head the Jharkhand High Court within a year of taking charge in Bengaluru. To fill the vacancy in Karnataka, the Collegium has recommended Justice Rao, who currently heads the Tripura High Court. Rao, who hails from the Telangana High Court and earlier served as a judge of the Telangana and Andhra Pradesh High Courts, will take over as Karnataka Chief Justice. Justice Vivek Singh Thakur, a judge of the Himachal Pradesh High Court, has been recommended as Chief Justice of the Tripura High Court, succeeding Rao. The Collegium’s resolutions will now be sent to the Union Ministry of Law and Justice. Once approved by the Centre, the appointments will be notified, and the judges will take oath in their respective High Courts.

headline: Himachal’s finances in deep crisis, debt exceeds 40% of GSDP, fiscal deficit breaches 3% limit
content: Shimla: Himachal Pradesh’s precarious financial position has emerged as a major concern, with outstanding liabilities exceeding 40% of its gross state domestic product (GSDP), a persistent revenue deficit, limited revenue-generating capacity and mounting expenditure commitments leaving little fiscal space for development.The state’s fiscal deficit is also projected to remain above the recommended borrowing limit, exposing the fragile state of its economy. Himachal Pradesh is among four states whose outstanding liabilities exceeded 40% of GSDP in 2025-26, alongside Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Punjab, according to the latest PRS Legislative Research report ‘State of State Finances 2026-27’.The assessment excludes 50-year interest-free loans extended by the Centre for capital expenditure. The consolidated debt of all states is 28% of GDP, lower than the 32.5% by March 2026 estimate of the 15th Finance Commission.Expenditure patterns further underline the financial stress. Himachal is among the states expected to spend 90% or more of their total expenditure on revenue items rather than asset creation. This is higher than the all-state average of 82%. About 88% of Himachal’s revenue receipts are spent on interest, salaries and pensions, leaving limited resources for fresh development projects.The state’s revenue deficit is estimated at 2.4% of GSDP in 2026-27, indicating that its revenue expenditure will substantially exceed its revenue receipts. The revenue deficit of all states in 2025-26 was 0.71% of GDP. This has been steadily increasing from the post-Covid low of 0.23% in 2022-23. Ten states have consistently reported a revenue deficit, and five have moved from surplus to deficit.More worrying for Himachal is the fiscal deficit, projected at 3.5% of GSDP after excluding Centre’s Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) loans, against the 3% limit recommended by the 16th Finance Commission. Himachal has budgeted zero receipts under the SASCI scheme for 2026-27. The hill state’s weak revenue base is another major concern. Its own tax revenue is estimated at just 5.5% of GSDP in 2026-27, considerably below the national average of 7%.State goods and services tax (SGST) is projected at 2.4% of GSDP, sales tax at 0.8%, excise duty at 1.1%, stamp duty at 0.2% and other sources at 0.9%. The subsidy burden also remains significant. According to 2024-25 audited figures, subsidies accounted for 4.6% of Himachal’s revenue receipts, while power subsidies constituted 50% of its total subsidy expenditure.The discontinuation of revenue deficit grants, as recommended by the 16th Finance Commission, could add to the state’s difficulties. The report specifically identifies Himachal Pradesh and Punjab as states likely to be affected by this change because of their recurring revenue deficits.Himachal Pradesh is estimated to spend 2% of revenue receipts in financial year 2026-27 on unconditional cash transfer schemes and the beneficiaries include women, farmers, the elderly, widows and persons with disabilities. Himachal’s financial predicament is compounded by its limited economic base and dependence on central transfers.The report’s findings underline the urgency of improving revenue mobilisation, controlling recurring expenditure and prioritising productive capital investment to prevent the state’s debt burden from becoming an even bigger obstacle to development.

headline: Keralam to form committee to probe PSC rank lists issued for posts without vacancies
content: The Keralam government on Wednesday decided to constitute a committee to examine the issues within the functioning of the state Public Service Commission (PSC). Headed by the Chief Secretary, the committee will investigate the commission's practice of conducting interviews and publishing rank lists for posts for which no vacancies exist. Addressing media personnel after the weekly Cabinet meeting, Chief Minister V D Satheesan said that the act of displaying rank lists comprising thousands of names without the availability of sufficient vacancies creates false hopes among job aspirants and that no government can carry on with such a system. He added that the state government would hold discussions with the Public Service Commission (PSC) to bring forth necessary changes and establish a proper system. He said that the review would also cover other departments to find a permanent solution. Commenting on the situation in government lower primary (LP) schools, the chief minister said the actual student-teacher ratio was 1:19 against the declared ratio of 1:30, with considerable variations across districts. (With inputs from PTI)

headline: Workers in high-risk jobs to receive shots against rabies in Tamil Nadu
content: CHENNAI Over a lakh persons belonging to high-risk occupational groups, including animal handlers and dog catchers of local bodies, in all 38 districts will receive Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) against rabies under the Tamil Nadu State Action Plan for Dog-Mediated Rabies Elimination (SAPRE) - Vision 2030. The State government has given the administrative sanction for implementation of the initiative at a cost of ₹2.22 crore, which will be met from the National Health Mission, Tamil Nadu, an order issued recently said. In just four months of 2026, Tamil Nadu records 2.63 lakh dog bites, 17 deaths In just four months of 2026, Tamil Nadu records 2.63 lakh dog bites, 17 deaths A total of 62,000 dog bite cases were recorded each in January and February, and it rose to 71,000 in March and dipping slightly to 68,000 in April; half of last year’s deaths has been recorded in just four months this year Gaps in anti-rabies treatment persist in Chennai’s health centres Gaps in anti-rabies treatment persist in Chennai’s health centres There is limited awareness about availability of vaccines at UPHCs and UCHCs; patients requiring Rabies Immunoglobulin are referred to nearest govt. tertiary care centres; officials say vaccines are available at health facilities in all zones The Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine noted that certain occupational groups are routinely exposed to dogs and other animals in the course of their duties. Provision of PrEP to such identified high-risk personnel will provide an additional layer of protection and strengthen the State’s rabies elimination strategy. The programme aims to provide PrEP to identified personnel of occupational groups having sustained risk of exposure to dogs and other potentially rabid animals. The main categories include sanitation workers, animal handlers and dog catchers of local bodies and eligible personnel of the Animal Husbandry Department involved in animal handling, dog catching, veterinary and para-veterinary activities. Eligibility criteria As per the National Guidelines on Rabies Prophylaxis, eligibility will be determined based on occupational exposure risk and the nature of duties performed. Based on the presently available department data, the preliminary beneficiary estimation was 1,29,009 - 1,21,844 local body sanitation workers, 3,324 local body animal handlers/dog catchers and 3,841 personnel attached to the Animal Husbandry department, the directorate said. Tamil Nadu sees 5.25 lakh dog bite cases, 28 rabies deaths so far in 2025 Tamil Nadu sees 5.25 lakh dog bite cases, 28 rabies deaths so far in 2025 In view of the rise in cases of dog bites — from 4.8 lakh last year — the Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine says the issue has to be tackled with inter-departmental coordination Tamil Nadu sees 5.25 lakh dog bite cases, 28 rabies deaths so far in 2025 storyline 1 The initiative will be implemented through designated government health facilities, including Primary Health Centres (PHC), Urban PHCs, government hospitals, and medical college hospitals. Identification of beneficiaries and mobilisation will be carried out by the respective local bodies and Animal Husbandry Department.
