headline: Vantara signs 10-year wildlife conservation pact with Madagascar to repatriate trafficked animals — All we know
content: Vantara has signed a 10-year agreement with Madagascar to help bring animals seized abroad back to their home country, support their rehabilitation, and, where possible, return them to the wild.The Greens Zoological Rescue and Rehabilitation Centre Society (Vantara), based in Jamnagar, Gujarat, and Madagascar’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD) signed the non-exclusive Memorandum of Understanding on wildlife conservation and animal welfare on November 24.The deal fulfils a commitment Vantara made to India’s CITES Management Authority on August 19. Under the agreement, Vantara will assist in the safe return of Malagasy animals seized overseas and support their rescue, rehabilitation, and veterinary care.New conservation centre in MadagascarBeyond repatriation, the partnership focuses on building Madagascar’s domestic conservation capacity. Vantara will help train local wildlife experts and may support the construction and establishment of a National Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation Centre.Planned as a national hub for conservation, research, and training, the centre will remain the property of the Republic of Madagascar and operate under MEDD’s authority on government-provided land.Why does Madagascar’s wildlife need urgent support?Madagascar is home to species found nowhere else on Earth, many of which are under severe threat. According to the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, 90% of lemur species in the country are threatened with extinction, and nearly a third are Critically Endangered.The country’s radiated tortoises face a similar crisis. The Turtle Survival Alliance estimates their wild population dropped by more than 47% between the late 1990s and 2013. Madagascar also lost roughly 29% of its tree cover between 2001 and 2023.Illegal wildlife trade compounds the problem, with Madagascar’s environment minister describing it as the second leading cause of biodiversity decline after habitat loss. Between January and April 2026 alone, rescuers in the country received more than 1,000 tortoises from six confiscation cases.Challenge of returning trafficked animalsBringing seized animals home is often a slow and complicated process. When Thai authorities intercepted 48 lemurs and more than 1,000 tortoises in 2024, 131 tortoises had already died in transit, and others did not survive the weeks that followed.While Thailand cared for the surviving animals and backed their return, there was no dedicated funding, and complex international permit procedures delayed flights back to Madagascar twice.Under the new pact, Vantara’s teams can assist at Madagascar’s request across different stages of an animal’s return, including health checks, disease screening, transport, quarantine, and post-arrival care.Vantara will also share scientific expertise, such as field research and genetic profiling, to help Madagascar decide which animals can be released into the wild and where, in line with IUCN guidelines.Every final decision will rest solely with the Government of Madagascar, advised by the country's CITES Scientific Authority.Focus on local expertise and in situ conservationThrough training, internships, specialist exchanges, and applied research, the partnership aims to ensure local teams can sustain conservation work long after rescued animals return.“Madagascar is a biodiversity hotspot of global importance, and our wildlife is part of who we are as a nation. These animals belong to the forests that shaped them,” said H.E. Nolave Luck Aristide Andriatsihala, Minister of Environment and Sustainable Development, Republic of Madagascar.“Protecting them takes cooperation across borders, and we are grateful to the countries and organisations, such as Vantara, who work with us to safeguard Madagascar's natural heritage,” Andriatsihala added.MEDD’s Director General of Environmental Governance Rakotondravoninala Valison Kiady said the partnership will focus on practical execution. “Vantara brings world-class expertise in animal rescue, veterinary care and welfare, and we look forward to working together to turn this commitment into concrete actions, from immediate deliverables to long-term, results-oriented programmes, all guided by science, regulations and international best practice,” Kiady said.Vantara Chief Executive Officer Vivaan Karani said the initiative reflects the organisation's focus on in situ conservation, or protecting animals in their natural home range.“Madagascar is home to some of the world’s most extraordinary and unique wildlife, and protecting these species in their natural habitats is central to our ten-year conservation strategy,” Karani said. “Our priority is to strengthen the people and institutions working to conserve wildlife in its country of origin. We thank the Government of Madagascar for this partnership and look forward to supporting its long-term conservation priorities, with every decision resting firmly with Madagascar.”

headline: Deepam row: SC to hear contempt plea against Tamil Nadu govt
content: New Delhi, The Supreme Court on Wednesday said it will hear the contempt plea and peruse the status report of the Tamil Nadu government over the issue of non-lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp at Deepathoon atop the Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai district.The contempt plea urged initiation of action against the Tamil Nadu government for allegedly failing to comply with its directions on lighting of the lamp.The matter was mentioned before a bench comprising Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi. During the proceedings, the counsel for the state government informed the bench that he was required to file a status report detailing the developments in the matter and urged the bench to take it up, pointing out that the traditional lamp had, unfortunately, not been lit at Deepathoon.A senior advocate, appearing for the petitioner seeking permission to light the lamp, termed the developments "most unfortunate".He submitted that the state government had informed the Madras High Court that prohibitory orders were in force and that customary practices did not permit the lighting of the lamp at the disputed location.Alleging deliberate non-compliance with the Supreme Court's directions, the petitioner's counsel argued that the flame should have been carried to Deepathoon and the lamp lit there.He also pointed out that the state government had repeatedly assured the high court, until the last moment, that it would comply with the court's directions.The counsel urged the bench to initiate suo motu contempt proceedings against the authorities concerned, alleging that the state government had circumvented the apex court's directions.He also referred to the review petition filed by the state government.When the senior advocate indicated that the petitioners would move a contempt petition, the bench said, "File it, and then we will see."The latest developments follow the Tamil Nadu government's failure to implement the top court's November 21 order permitting the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp to be lit at Deepathoon, a stone pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill, on November 24 as a one-time measure.The dispute centres on the traditional practice of lighting the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the hilltop location and the state authorities' objections to implementing the direction, citing law-and-order restrictions and customary practices.This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

headline: Oxford-led trial finds twice-yearly cholesterol shot reduces heart risks
content: A cholesterol-lowering injection administered just twice a year reduced the risk of heart attacks, strokes and other major cardiovascular events in a large clinical trial led by the University of Oxford. The findings could mark an important development in heart disease prevention, particularly for people who already have cardiovascular disease and struggle to keep their cholesterol levels under control. The treatment, called inclisiran and marketed as Leqvio by pharmaceutical company Novartis, demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in major cardiovascular events when added to standard cholesterol-lowering treatment. What the study found The Phase III ORION-4 trial involved more than 16,000 participants with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), a condition in which fatty deposits build up inside artery walls and increase the risk of heart attacks and strokes. The study found that inclisiran, when used alongside standard treatment, reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events. These included: Death from coronary heart diseaseNon-fatal heart attacksNon-fatal ischaemic strokesUrgent procedures to restore blood flow to the heart “These findings are particularly important given the substantial burden of cardiovascular disease and the continued need for effective approaches to reducing cardiovascular risk,” said Louise Bowman, Professor of Medicine and Clinical Trials, and Honorary Consultant Physician (Lipidology), Oxford Population Health, and lead ORION-4 investigator. The trial met its primary endpoint, although Novartis has yet to disclose the exact reduction in cardiovascular risk. Led by Oxford Population Health in collaboration with the TIMI Study Group, the trial is among the largest studies examining cardiovascular outcomes from an RNA-based cholesterol-lowering treatment. Full findings are expected to be published in the first half of 2027. How the cholesterol shot works Unlike conventional cholesterol-lowering medicines such as statins, inclisiran uses a technology called small interfering RNA (siRNA) to reduce the production of a protein known as PCSK9. This protein breaks down receptors in the liver that help remove low-density lipoprotein (LDL), commonly called bad cholesterol, from the bloodstream. By reducing PCSK9 production, inclisiran allows more of these receptors to remain available, helping the liver clear LDL cholesterol more effectively. The injection is administered by a healthcare professional according to the following schedule: An initial doseA second dose after three monthsOne injection every six months thereafter Earlier research found that inclisiran could lower LDL cholesterol by around 50 per cent over 18 months. The ORION-4 findings are significant because they provide the first cardiovascular outcomes evidence for an siRNA therapy in patients with established ASCVD. Why it matters for India The findings could be particularly relevant for India, where high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease have emerged as major health challenges. A 2026 analysis of the ICMR-INDIAB (Indian Council of Medical Research-India Diabetes) study, published in the Journal of Clinical Lipidology, found that 87.3 per cent of Indian adults had dyslipidaemia, a condition characterised by unhealthy levels of fats (lipids) in the bloodstream. This usually means having too much bad cholesterol or triglycerides, or too little good cholesterol. The study examined over 23,600 participants and highlighted how widespread the problem was across different population groups. The study found that dyslipidaemia affected 89 per cent of people in urban areas and 86.5 per cent in rural areas, with a higher prevalence among women (91.1 per cent) than men (83.5 per cent). The condition was also widespread among younger adults, with prevalence peaking in the 30-39 age group. Notably, around 40 per cent of people without diabetes, hypertension or obesity also had abnormal blood lipid levels, suggesting that cholesterol-related risks extend beyond those traditionally considered vulnerable. The findings suggest that cholesterol-related risks are not restricted to older people or those with existing metabolic conditions, making early screening and prevention increasingly important. The wider cardiovascular burden is equally concerning. According to the Beat by Beat 2025 report by BM Birla Heart Hospital, India accounts for nearly 20 per cent of heart attack deaths across more than 190 countries. The report also highlighted that cardiovascular diseases account for nearly 25 per cent of all deaths in India, with around 60 per cent of these deaths occurring prematurely. India's cardiovascular death rate stands at 272 per 100,000 people, compared with the global average of 235. Elevated LDL cholesterol was identified as one of the important metabolic contributors to cardiovascular mortality, alongside high blood pressure and rising blood sugar levels. What this means for patients One of the potential advantages of inclisiran is its dosing schedule, which could make long-term cholesterol management easier for patients who struggle with daily medication. However, the findings do not mean that patients can replace their existing cholesterol medicines with an injection. The ORION-4 trial evaluated inclisiran alongside standard lipid-lowering treatment, particularly in people with established cardiovascular disease. The full trial results will also be important in understanding the extent of the benefits and the treatment's wider clinical implications. For India, where the burden of cardiovascular disease remains high, the development offers another potential tool for reducing heart-related risks. However, early diagnosis, regular cholesterol screening, timely treatment and lifestyle changes remain central to preventing heart attacks and strokes.

headline: Missing BSF jawan’s body found in Kushiyara River in Assam after two days
content: The body of a 32-year-old Border Security Force (BSF) jawan who went missing while chasing suspected cattle smugglers near the India-Bangladesh border in Assam’s Cachar district has been recovered from the Kushiyara River on Wednesday morning, two days after the incident, a senior BSF official said.Constable (GD) K Venu, a resident of Telangana and posted at Harinagar Border Outpost (BOP) in Assam's Katigorah, went missing on Monday. BSF Mizoram and Cachar Frontier deputy inspector general (DIG) Ahsan Shahedi confirmed that Venu’s body was recovered at around 8.20 am on Wednesday near Steamerghat in Sribhumi district, downstream along the river.“Sad news. His dead body has been retrieved from River Kushiyara near Steamerghat, Sribhumi, after it was found floating downstream,” Sahedi said in a message to HT.The DIG said the initial investigation suggests that there were no external injuries on the body. However, he added that the body will be sent to Silchar Medical College and Hospital (SMCH) for a postmortem examination.The body will subsequently be taken to his home state by air, accompanied by BSF officers, where he will be accorded state honours.The jawan’s disappearance had triggered speculation that he might have been taken into Bangladesh. However, the BSF denied receiving any such information from the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB).“No, it is not true. He has not been traced yet. Comdt-level meetings with BGB also held but no positive outcome as yet. Search is still ongoing,” the DIG had told HT on Tuesday, responding to claims that the jawan was in Bangladesh.The incident occurred early Monday near Harinagar BOP, when BSF personnel received specific intelligence inputs about the movement of four to five persons suspected of attempting to smuggle cattle through the border area.Teams from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), river police, and BSF personnel subsequently launched a search operation in the river to trace the missing jawan. The search continued until his body was recovered on Wednesday morning.

headline: 120 seats and Gandhi family turf: Why Amethi, Raebareli are testing Congress-SP ties
content: NEW DELHI: Differences over seat-sharing have surfaced between the Congress and Samajwadi Party ahead of the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. The Congress is demanding 120 constituencies, including the Gandhi family's traditional strongholds of Amethi and Raebareli, and is unwilling to settle for fewer seats, news agency ANI reported, citing party sources.Congress conveyed its demand during a meeting with SP leaders in Delhi, where it submitted a list of 120 constituencies it wants to contest, sources told ANI.The list reportedly includes two seats in Saharanpur, where the SP has already announced its candidates, as well as several constituencies in traditional Congress stronghold Raebareli and Amethi, some of which have sitting SP MLAs.The demands could further complicate negotiations between the two INDIA bloc allies.Why Amethi and Raebareli matterAmethi and Raebareli have long been considered the Gandhi family's political turf, with both constituencies playing a significant role in the family's electoral legacy.Amethi's association with the Gandhi family began with Sanjay Gandhi, who won the Lok Sabha seat in 1980. After his death, his brother Rajiv Gandhi won the constituency three consecutive times. The seat later passed to Sonia Gandhi, who won it in 1999 on her political entry, before handing it over to her son Rahul Gandhi.Rahul won Amethi three times, in 2004, 2009 and 2014, before losing to BJP's actor-turned-politician Smriti Irani in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections.Raebareli, meanwhile, has been associated with the family since the first-ever Lok Sabha elections in 1952, when Feroze Gandhi won the seat. He retained it in 1957 as well. After his death, his wife and former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi represented the constituency, winning in 1967, 1971 and 1980.The seat remained with the family from 2004 onwards, with Sonia Gandhi winning it in four consecutive Lok Sabha elections before making way for Rahul Gandhi, who won Raebareli in the 2024 general elections.While the upcoming contest is for the Uttar Pradesh assembly and not the Lok Sabha, the seats in these two districts continue to hold symbolic significance for the Gandhi family.SP stresses on 'winnability'Meanwhile, SP supremo Akhilesh Yadav has stressed that "winnability" and the larger objective of defeating the BJP should guide the seat-sharing arrangement.In a post on X, Akhilesh called for mutual understanding between the alliance partners and said candidates should be selected based on their electoral prospects. He also emphasised the need for consensus candidates representing the PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) framework on every seat to take on the BJP.The differences have also triggered sharp reactions within the Congress. Saharanpur MP Imran Masood questioned the SP's reported offer of just 26 seats to the Congress, asking, "Are we beggars?"While the Congress has drawn a line at 120 seats, Akhilesh has indicated that discussions should continue, with the focus on identifying candidates capable of winning rather than dividing constituencies strictly between the two parties.Get the latest India News and Live updates. headline: 'Reel blocked, visa cancelled': Dhruv Rathee hits out at Centre after Saurav Das denied flight to London
content: NEW DELHI: YouTuber and influencer Dhruv Rathee on Tuesday criticised the Narendra Modi led BJP government. In a post on X he alleged that those who speak against PM Modi face a range of consequences, including blocked social media content, legal cases and detention.In a post on X Rathee said, “If you criticise Narendra Modi — your reel will be blocked in India, your visa will be cancelled (if you are foreign citizen), you will be stopped from going outside India (if you are Indian citizen), you will get fake court cases on you, you will get illegally detained / arrested / kidnapped by police.”He also alleged that critics could face “fake charges” from the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), ending the post with the sarcastic remark and a clown emoji, “Mother of Democracy!”Rathee’s post came amid two recent developments involving people associated with criticism of the government.On Monday, a Delhi court issued a non-bailable warrant (NBW) against Rathee in a 2018 defamation case filed by Vikas Sanskrityayan, also known as Vikas Pandey. The case relates to a video uploaded by Rathee on his YouTube channel, which the complainant alleges was defamatory.Earlier this month, the court had issued fresh bailable warrants after a process server reported that Rathee’s residence was locked when he attempted to serve notice. The court had also issued fresh summons to Rathee at his Gurugram address.In another incident, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Saurav Das alleged that he was stopped from boarding a flight to London at Delhi airport, where he was scheduled to deliver a lecture at the University of Oxford.Das said he had been invited by Oxford, Cambridge, the London School of Economics and the University of Edinburgh to speak about the CJP movement. He accused the government of preventing him from travelling because it feared his views would reach international academic institutions.Rathee’s post linked the developments to what he described as consequences faced by people who criticise the prime minister.Get the latest India News and Live updates. headline: 76% of parents are uncomfortable with AI chatbots providing mental health therapy to children, Harvard st
content: Artificial intelligence chatbots are becoming an easy place for young people to turn when they feel anxious, lonely or emotionally overwhelmed. They are available at any hour, respond almost instantly and do not require an appointment. But when it comes to using these tools for children's mental health treatment, most parents are not convinced.A new study involving researchers from Harvard Medical School, Boston Children's Hospital and RAND Corporation has found that 76% of parents are uncomfortable with the idea of AI-led behavioural therapy for their children. The findings have been published in JAMA Pediatrics on November 2, 2026.The researchers surveyed 572 parents, in November 2025, who had at least one child between the ages of 5 and 17.According to the findings, 47.2% of parents said they were not comfortable at all with AI-led behavioural therapy for their children, while another 28.8% said they were not too comfortable. Only 16.2% were somewhat comfortable and 7.8% were very comfortable with the idea.Why parents are hesitant to trust AI with children's mental healthDiagnostic accuracy was the biggest concern. About 58.5% of parents identified it as an important factor when considering AI-led therapy for their children.Another 49.4% were concerned about the level of empathy a chatbot could provide. Around 46.8% wanted the treatment to be recommended by a medical professional, while 43.7% prioritised confidentiality and privacy.Interestingly, practical considerations such as cost, flexible appointment timings and waiting periods ranked lower.Rosemary Martoma, the study's first author and an instructor in pediatrics at Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital, said parents were particularly focused on diagnostic accuracy. She told Alvin Powell, Harvard Staff Writer, that it made sense for parents to be cautious about whether children would receive appropriate care through these tools.Having a child who had received behavioural therapy in the previous 12 months was associated with greater parental comfort. However, simply using AI chatbots for everyday activities did not make parents more comfortable with AI-led mental health treatment.Children are already turning to AI for mental health adviceOne of the more concerning aspects of the discussion is that children and teenagers may already be using general-purpose chatbots to discuss their emotional problems, even when their parents are unaware.The JAMA Pediatrics paper refers to a separate 2025 national survey in which 19.2% of young people aged 12 to 21 reported using AI chatbots for mental health advice. Some did so without telling their parents or healthcare professionals.This raises a different question for families. Even if parents do not want AI to replace a therapist, children may still be using these tools to discuss loneliness, anxiety, relationships or other personal concerns.General-purpose AI chatbots are not the same as clinically evaluated mental health treatment tools. A chatbot may respond confidently, but that does not mean it can accurately understand a child's emotional condition or recognise when professional intervention is needed.Therapist shortage is adding to the problemThe hesitation around AI comes at a time when access to child mental health services remains a major challenge in the US.In the Harvard Gazette report on the research, Martoma pointed to the shortage of professionals providing paediatric behavioural healthcare. She said children with more serious concerns can wait several months for appointments when their needs go beyond what a primary-care doctor can manage during a short consultation.A report by the Association for Behavioral Healthcare also found that young patients waited an average of four months for initial assessments, therapy or psychiatric prescription management.This shortage is one reason AI-based mental health tools are attracting attention. They offer the possibility of immediate access, particularly for families who struggle to find appointments.But availability does not automatically make a tool suitable for treatment. Children's mental health care often requires clinical assessment, an understanding of family circumstances and the ability to recognise when a situation needs urgent attention.Can AI become part of children's mental health care?There are already efforts to develop chatbots specifically for mental health support. One example is Therabot, developed by researchers at Dartmouth.However, the Harvard and Boston Children's Hospital researchers say the discussion should involve more than technology developers. Parents, children, therapists and doctors need to be part of decisions about how these tools are evaluated and used.The question is no longer simply whether children will use AI to discuss their feelings. It is whether these tools can be made safe, accountable and clinically appropriate before they become a more established part of mental health care.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. headline: ‘Acted on a grudge’: AAP sarpanch’s husband shot at in Punjab over drug tip-off
content: The husband of a sitting Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) sarpanch was allegedly shot at in Punjab's Tarn Taran district by two brothers who suspected his family of tipping off the police about their associate, who was arrested in a drug case. The incident occurred around 12.30 pm on Tuesday, November 24, when Sukhbir Singh, 42, was travelling on a motorcycle toward Tarn Taran city with his wife, the Sarpanch of Daleke village. According to the police report registered at Sadar Tarn Taran police station (FIR No. 331), Mangal Singh alias Manga and Udham Singh alias Udhe, residents of Palasaur Kalan, rammed their motorcycle into Sukhbir's bike to force the couple to stop. "With the intention to kill me, they opened fire, vandalised my motorcycle, and issued death threats before fleeing,” Sukhbir Singh said in his complaint to the police. According to investigators, an associate of the accused, Amritpal Singh of Jodha village, who also has his maternal home in Daleke, allegedly sold drugs supplied by the two brothers in the area. The police arrested Amritpal and sent him to jail, and the accused allegedly suspected Sukhbir and his wife's family of tipping off the police, leading to Amritpal's arrest. "The motive behind the attack is a grudge held by the accused after their drug peddler associate was arrested and jailed by the police," said Rajpal Singh, Assistant Sub-Inspector and the investigating officer in the case. "We have registered an FIR under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Arms Act, and further investigation is underway to nab the culprits."

headline: RBI to widen market for government securities: DG Jain
content: MUMBAI: RBI is seeking to broaden retail participation in govt securities (G-secs) and improve secondary-market liquidity by making it easier for individual investors to access the market and encouraging primary dealers (PDs) to expand their market-making activities.Speaking at Primary Dealers’ Association of India (PDAI) Seminar 2026 here on Monday, RBI deputy governor Rohit Jain outlined measures to widen the investor base and distribute trading activity more evenly across the yield curve at a time when there is a drop in demand from long-term institutional investors.“It has been observed that demand from banks, insurers and pension funds for long-term sovereign debt has marginally declined, with insurance and pension funds shifting towards more of equity exposure. This has structurally reduced such demand for govt securities,” said Jain.To widen the investor base, Jain said PDs could play a greater role by acting as active market makers under the scheme, conducting awareness campaigns and educating retail investors about the benefits of these instruments. They could also tailor bond offerings to retail investors, including shorter-tenor STRIPS (Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities), which are relatively easier to understand.To improve secondary-market liquidity, RBI has reduced the frequency of benchmark G-sec issuances and increased the volume offered in each auction. These measures have helped improve trading liquidity, but it remains lower than in other countries.Jain said PDs should increase market-making activity, particularly by providing two-way quotes in off-the-run securities.Money habits form by age 7. headline: Punjab teacher spent 18 years planting around 10,000 trees along roads, schools and public spaces, starti
content: What began with 125 saplings, a bucket of water and a simple concern for children walking under the scorching summer sun has grown into an extraordinary 18-year mission. At 56, Ranjit Singh Chinna, a government schoolteacher from Punjab's Gurdaspur district, has planted and nurtured around 10,000 fruit-bearing and medicinal trees across highways, village roads and public spaces.Popularly known as the 'Tree Man of Gurdaspur', Chinna has spent nearly two decades making roads greener, creating shaded spaces and improving his surroundings. His journey has not been driven by a large organisation or an elaborate environmental campaign. Instead, it has been powered by personal commitment, his own resources and the belief that even small efforts can make a difference.Today, his plantation work extends across several parts of the border district, while his contribution to society goes beyond planting trees. From cleaning public spaces to respectfully burying dead animals and birds found along roads, he has made community service an important part of his life.A road without trees gave birth to a green missionChinna's journey began in 2007 when he noticed something missing along the road connecting his native village, Chinna Railwala, with Naushera Magha Singh. The approximately one-kilometre stretch had no trees, leaving children returning from school and college exposed to the harsh summer heat. Rather than waiting for someone else to address the problem, he decided to do something himself.He planted 125 saplings along the road over three months. However, planting them was only the beginning. With no proper water supply available, he carried water in a bucket and watered each sapling himself. Recalling those early days, Chinna told The New Indian Express, “This road is around one kilometre, so I planted 125 trees in the span of three months and then used to water them with my own bucket, as I had no source to water them otherwise.”The modest beginning gradually developed into a much larger environmental effort. What started as an attempt to provide shade to children became a lifelong commitment to improving the district's green cover.From a bucket to a tractor, the work kept growingAs the number of saplings increased, manually carrying water became increasingly difficult. Chinna came up with a practical solution by installing a 500-litre water tank on his motorcycle, using a tyre as its base. This allowed him to transport water and irrigate more plants. However, a back problem eventually made it difficult for him to continue using the motorcycle for the task. He then shifted the water tank to his tractor trolley, which he now uses to water the trees.Explaining the change, he said, “After that, due to my back problem, I have installed that tank in my tractor trolley and thus now irrigate the plants.” Over the years, his plantation efforts expanded beyond national highways to village link roads and public spaces. He has planted trees around railway stations, schools, cremation grounds and bus stands.He particularly focuses on planting saplings between June and August. Whenever he identifies suitable land for plantation, he raises around 400 to 500 saplings. The effort requires considerable personal investment, with Chinna spending approximately Rs 60,000 to Rs 65,000 every year on his green mission.His idea of service extends beyond planting treesFor Chinna, environmental responsibility does not end with making an area greener. He has also taken up several tasks that many people might overlook, including clearing unwanted vegetation and ensuring that dead animals and birds found along roads are properly buried. For the past 15 years, he has been involved in collecting and burying animal and bird carcasses. He considers this an important responsibility because decomposing bodies can create public health concerns and attract harmful bacteria and other pathogens.He also believes that leaving dead animals exposed or throwing them into garbage dumps is disrespectful. In his view, animals deserve dignity even after death. Explaining why he undertakes this work, Chinna said that removing carcasses also helps prevent accidents, as motorists sometimes make sudden manoeuvres to avoid bodies lying on busy roads. During the rainy season, he additionally clears congress grass along village link roads. His efforts also include cleaning stretches used by devotees after religious processions.His commitment to public service was visible even before his tree-planting initiative began. According to The Tribune, between 2005 and 2012, he served drinking water to passengers at Chhina railway station every day, without missing a single day. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he also offered to transport infected patients to hospitals using his vehicle.The 'Tree Man of Gurdaspur' believes small efforts matterChinna's dedication has earned him recognition from several social and voluntary organisations. He has also received the Bhai Kanhaiya Award for excellence in social service. Despite the appreciation, he believes the real reward lies in helping others rather than receiving awards. His guiding thought is a simple question: “What are you doing for others?”He also recognises that one individual cannot transform an entire district's environment alone. According to The Tribune, Gurdaspur has limited forest cover, and Chinna believes greater participation from NGOs and social organisations could help expand the district's green spaces. For now, he continues his work with the resources available to him, identifying suitable locations, raising saplings, watering them and ensuring that they survive.At 56, his journey offers a refreshing perspective on environmental activism. It does not always require a massive campaign, expensive machinery or institutional backing to begin making a difference. Sometimes, it starts with noticing a problem on a familiar road, planting a few saplings and returning every day with a bucket of water. Nearly 10,000 trees later, Chinna's efforts have turned that small act of concern into a mission that continues to benefit people, animals and the environment.You use AI every day. headline: Bhagwant Mann questions BJP-Akali Dal alliance, alleges political interests behind reunion
content: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Singh Mann on Tuesday criticised the BJP's renewed alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal), alleging that the two parties had joined hands to protect their political interests rather than work for Punjab. He questioned the rationale behind the reunion, citing their past disagreements over farm laws, Chandigarh, water-sharing issues and Sikh institutions. Describing the alliance as a political arrangement, Mann alleged that both parties were seeking to regain lost political ground. In a statement shared on X, he said the people of Punjab would remember the parties' record during their previous tenure in government. Referring to the farmers' agitation against the three farm laws, Mann alleged that the Badal family had initially supported the legislation but changed its position after the protests gained wider support. He cited the resignation of Harsimrat Kaur Badal from the Union Cabinet and the Akali Dal's subsequent opposition to the laws as evidence of this shift. The chief minister also questioned the Akali Dal's decision to align with the BJP despite its earlier criticism of the party over issues concerning Punjab. These included the proposed changes to Panjab University's governance, Chandigarh's status, the state's water rights, and the management of Sikh institutions. The 2007-2017 Akali-BJP government Mann also referred to the 2007-2017 Akali-BJP government, alleging that the period was marked by the drug menace and incidents of sacrilege. He said the two parties had governed Punjab together for 10 years and had failed to address several issues affecting the state. Questioning the political consistency of the alliance partners, Mann said they had previously indicated that they would contest elections independently but had now decided to come together. He alleged that the partnership was an attempt to protect political families and their positions. The chief minister contrasted the BJP-Akali Dal alliance with the Aam Aadmi Party's governance agenda, saying his party's alliance was with Punjab's 3.25 crore people, including farmers, women, young people and ordinary families. Citing the state government's initiatives, Mann referred to free electricity, canal water for agriculture, Mohalla Clinics, health cards offering coverage of up to ₹10 lakh and more than 78,000 government jobs. He claimed the jobs had been provided without bribes or political recommendations. He also highlighted the government's Schools of Eminence initiative, saying students from these institutions were performing well in competitive examinations, including NEET. Mann said the AAP would take its government schemes and achievements to households across Punjab. He reiterated that the party would pursue what he described as positive politics, without seeking support on religious or caste lines. The chief minister also referred to the political history of Punjab between 2002 and 2022, when the Congress and the Akali-BJP alliance governed the state for much of the period. He alleged that these parties had sufficient opportunities to address Punjab's challenges but had failed to present a roadmap for its development.

headline: BJP-SAD alliance will rid Punjab of gangsters, drug menace: Saini
content: Chandigarh: Haryana chief minister Nayab Singh Saini on Tuesday described the BJP-Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) alliance as a “natural alliance of hearts”, saying the partnership would give Punjab a new direction, strengthen the state and safeguard the dignity and interests of its people.Interacting with mediapersons in Gurgaon, Saini said the alliance was not merely a political arrangement but a partnership aimed at taking Punjab forward on the path of development and fulfilling people’s aspirations.He said ending gangsterism and the drug menace, safeguarding farmers’ interests, ensuring the safety and dignity of women and working for the welfare of the poor would be among the alliance’s key priorities.Saini called upon the people of Punjab to unite and contribute towards strengthening the state and giving it a new direction.He congratulated Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and BJP national president Nitin Nabin for taking the initiative to forge the alliance in the larger interest of Punjab.Recalling the longstanding association between the BJP and SAD, the CM said Modi was carrying forward the relationship established during the tenure of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee and senior BJP leader LK Advani.

headline: SAD-BJP revival prompts voices in Punjab Congress to explore alliance
content: Chandigarh: The revival of the SAD-BJP alliance has prompted sections of Punjab Congress to explore the possibility of joining hands with INDIA bloc parties active in the state ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections. They believe an alliance could help Congress address the challenge of a multi-cornered contest.The issue figured in discussions at a meeting of Punjab Congress Election Committee on Tuesday, where leaders also deliberated on the possible electoral implications of the SAD-BJP alliance and the party’s strategy to counter the two parties.According to sources, some senior leaders favoured exploring an understanding with Left parties, including Communist Party of India (Marxist), which is part of the INDIA bloc and has a presence in Punjab. They felt that the Left parties’ links with farmers’ and employees’ unions could be useful in reaching out to these sections. However, no decision on an alliance was taken at the meeting.The discussions come amid efforts by several political groups in Punjab to explore possible electoral arrangements ahead of the Assembly elections. Akali Dal Waris Punjab De, SAD (Punar Surjit) and Bahujan Samaj Party have held preliminary discussions on a possible alliance. The Simranjit Singh Mann-led SAD (Amritsar) has also been involved in discussions.The Congress meeting also saw a detailed discussion on the revival of the SAD-BJP alliance. Party leaders felt the tie-up could offer Congress an opportunity to consolidate its position, especially in rural areas, particularly by highlighting the farming community’s opposition to the three farm laws. They stressed the need for an aggressive campaign against BJP’s policies and Akali Dal’s record in Punjab.Leaders were of the view that Congress should reach out to the public and highlight what they described as BJP’s anti-farmer and anti-Punjab policies, particularly the three farm laws. They suggested reminding people that Akali Dal had quit National Democratic Alliance (NDA) in 2020 in protest against the legislation and questioning what had changed since then to bring the two parties together again. Some leaders felt that resentment among the farming community over the farm laws could help Congress strengthen its position in rural constituencies.The leaders also stressed the need to highlight the SAD-BJP govt’s 10-year tenure in Punjab, from 2007 to 2017, which they claimed witnessed an escalation in the drug problem. They suggested raising the issues of sacrilege and the police firing incidents of 2015 as part of the campaign against SAD. BJP’s record at the Centre, particularly what it had done for Punjab during its 13 years in power, was another issue the leaders suggested should be taken to the people. They felt this should also form an important part of the Congress campaign against the renewed SAD-BJP alliance.Apart from political strategy, the meeting also discussed candidate selection. Leaders shared their views on prospective candidates and agreed that the state unit would send its suggestions to AICC. The recommendations would be prepared on the basis of individual inputs and survey reports before being forwarded to the Screening Committee. Leaders stressed the need to field candidates with a good reputation and a clean image, while providing greater opportunities to young leaders. They felt that, alongside its experienced senior leadership, the party should make room for younger faces with a clean public image.

headline: Punjab grappling with 42 lakh tonnes of legacy waste | Hindustan Times
content: Around 42.76 lakh metric tonnes (MT) of legacy waste is still lying untreated at dumping sites across Punjab, while 409 tonnes of fresh municipal garbage remains unprocessed every day, according to the latest compliance affidavit filed by the state government before the National Green Tribunal (NGT).This latest disclosure follows the NGT’s July-2024 direction asking Punjab to pay ₹1,000 crore in environmental compensation to the Central Pollution Control Board for alleged failures in managing legacy waste and untreated sewage. The Supreme Court stayed the tribunal’s order in September 2024.The affidavit, submitted by Punjab chief secretary KAP Sinha on November 14 and uploaded on the tribunal’s website on November 21, reveals that while Punjab processes nearly 91% of its daily municipal solid waste, the accumulated garbage and inadequate processing capacity continue to pose a serious environmental challenge.Of the cumulative 95.88 lakh MT of legacy waste at urban local body (ULB) dumping sites, only 53.12 lakh MT has been remediated, leaving 42.76 lakh MT untreated. While 126 of the state’s 166 ULBs have completed remediation, work remains underway in 40 others. The government has set January 2028 as the deadline to clear the remaining dumps.Legacy waste refers to garbage accumulated over several years at dumping sites. Its prolonged presence poses environmental and public health risks through leachate, landfill fires, foul odour and contamination of soil and groundwater.The NGT had earlier flagged the disposal of around 403 tonnes per day (TPD) of unprocessed mixed waste at landfill sites. It had identified Tarn Taran, Sangrur, Pathankot, Patiala, Ludhiana and Jalandhar among the urban local bodies contributing to the problem. The latest affidavit acknowledges a processing gap of 409 TPD, indicating that the challenge of managing fresh waste remains unresolved.Punjab’s 166 ULBs generate approximately 4,309 TPD of municipal solid waste, of which around 3,900 TPD (90.51%) is reportedly being processed. However, large accumulations of legacy waste continue to pose a challenge in Amritsar, Jalandhar, Ludhiana and Kharar, with the government claiming that focused interventions are underway at these sites.Gaps in biodegradable, recyclable waste managementThe affidavit also highlights deficiencies in the management of biodegradable and recyclable waste. Of the 2,291 tonnes of biodegradable waste generated per day, around 1,931 TPD is being processed through composting and other mechanisms.Similarly, material recovery facilities (MRFs) handle around 1,076 TPD of dry recyclable waste against the generated 1,717 TPD. The government has acknowledged a processing gap of approximately 253 tonnes per day after accounting for material recovered through other channels.Deputy commissioners and municipal commissioners are being directed to strengthen monitoring of waste collection, segregation and processing and ensure compliance with the tribunal’s directions.Sewage treatment another challengeWastewater management also remains a challenge in Punjab. The state generates around 2,286.91 million litres of sewage per day, but treats only 2,038.80 million litres per day (MLD), leaving a gap of 248.11 MLD.Of the 172 sewage treatment plants (STPs), 147 are reportedly complying with prescribed quality parameters, four are non-compliant, 19 are undergoing stabilisation, one is under maintenance and another is being upgraded.The government cited the commissioning of nine STPs, with a combined capacity of 45.50 MLD, between February and October this year. Another 37 plants, with a combined capacity of 206.40 MLD, are under construction, while proposals for 27 additional STPs, with a capacity of 127.73 MLD, are at the tendering or planning stage.

headline: Punjab sends 4-doctor panel for director, health services post
content: Chandigarh: With the term of the present director of health services (DHS), Suman Singh, ending on Tuesday, Punjab has sent a panel of four doctors for the post. The main contenders are two senior doctors from GMSH-16.Names in the panel include Paramjeet Singh, deputy medical superintendent at GMSH-16; Harneet Sandhu, a radiologist at the same hospital with 29 months of service left; Sangeeta Jain, a senior medical officer from Mohali; and Vivek Chopra, head of the department of paediatrics at GMSH-16.Suman Singh, who has been serving for the past five years, received a one-year extension last year after reaching retirement age. She is slated to retire on Nov 30. Her term in the UT ended on Nov 23, while Nov 30 marks her retirement from Punjab service.Eligibility norms for the panel stipulate that candidates must not exceed 56 years of age — a threshold raised from 55 years in the previous recruitment round. Of the four doctors on the list, only two meet the 56-year cap.Under the Punjab Reorganisation Act of 1966, the position of DHS has traditionally been filled from the Punjab Civil Medical Services quota. While applications were invited nationwide in 2025 following changes to UT recruitment rules, the administration restricted applications to Punjab this time around.The development has also revived longstanding friction over career progression for UT cadre doctors. Since central service rules were drafted in April 2022, senior UT cadre doctors have sought consideration for top posts such as DHS and medical superintendent. However, a previous Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) plea by a medical superintendent was dismissed because the rules had not been notified.

headline: BJP-Akali Dal alliance in Punjab will focus on tackling gangsterism, says Haryana CM Saini
content: Gurgaon: Haryana chief minister Nayab Singh Saini on Tuesday described BJP’s renewed partnership with Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) as a “natural alliance” and an “alliance of hearts” rooted in Punjab’s interests. The parties announced their alliance for the upcoming Punjab elections, six years after SAD walked out over the farm laws. Saini’s remarks come as BJP and SAD are seeking to underline a shared political agenda for Punjab, with issues of law and order, drugs, farmers’ welfare and governance likely to form key planks of their pitch to voters. He called upon people in Punjab to unite and contribute towards strengthening the state.While interacting with reporters in the city, the Haryana CM credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and BJP national president Nitin Nabin for taking the initiative to bring the two parties together, saying the alliance was formed keeping Punjab’s interests in mind. He also invoked the partnership between BJP and SAD during the tenure of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee and senior BJP leader LK Advani, describing the current alliance as a continuation of their longstanding political relationship.136133073The two parties would work together to restore the state’s direction, strengthen its economy and “safeguard people’s dignity”, Saini said, adding the partnership was not merely aimed at electoral politics but at addressing Punjab’s key challenges and fulfilling people’s aspirations. The alliance, he said, would focus on tackling gangsterism and the drug menace, protecting farmers’ interests, ensuring women’s safety and dignity, and working for the welfare of the poor. He also extended greetings on Guru Nanak Dev’s Prakash Parv. He said the Guru’s teachings of service, equality, brotherhood and compassion remained relevant in strengthening social harmony.

headline: SAD-BJP tie-up revives political activity in Fazilka, Abohar
content: Celebrations broke out at the office of former minister Surjit Kumar Jyani here on Tuesday following the announcement of the SAD-BJP alliance. Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) leaders also joined BJP workers in welcoming the development.Jyani, who had long been a strong supporter of the alliance, had even publicly advocated its revival. SAD leader Savi Kathpal also welcomed the announcement, expressing confidence that the alliance would win the Assembly elections and form the next government in Punjab.Jyani said not even a single brick had been added to the development works initiated during the previous SAD-BJP government in Fazilka. He claimed to have a comprehensive development plan for the town and said several pending projects could be taken up if the alliance returned to power.He said Punjab would benefit from a “triple-engine government”, as the BJP was in power at the Centre and the people of Fazilka had also elected a BJP-led civic body in the previous municipal elections.Meanwhile, Abohar MLA Sandeep Jakhar also welcomed the alliance, describing it as one of the oldest, most trusted and natural political partnerships. He said the alliance would give a fresh impetus to development in Punjab.Asked whether he would contest the next Assembly elections, Jakhar said he was definitely willing to contest on a BJP ticket if the party nominated him.He said his uncle, former Punjab BJP president Sunil Jakhar, had always favoured the restoration of the SAD-BJP alliance and that his wish had now been fulfilled. He expressed confidence that the alliance would form the next government in Punjab.Notably, Sandeep Jakhar contested the 2022 Assembly elections from Abohar on a Congress ticket and won despite a strong AAP wave in the state. However, the Congress suspended him on August 16, 2023, over allegations of anti-party activities, including his alleged failure to participate in party programmes and remarks against the party leadership.

headline: Congress to stage protest marches across country against 'vote chori' on Constitution Day
content: New Delhi: The Congress will hold protest marches against "vote chori" across the country on November 26 to mark Constitution Day, with party chief Mallikarjun Kharge set to participate in such a march in Lucknow. .The Congress has said that when a citizen's vote is stolen, every other right guaranteed by the Constitution becomes meaningless. .Congress general secretary Organisation K C Venugopal said in a statement that this fight is not about any one party, but about whether India will remain a democracy. .Kharge will join the Samvidhan Raksha March in Lucknow on November 26. .He said the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, placed before the nation documented evidence of "vote chori". .He highlighted "fake and duplicate" entries in Mahadevapura, systematic attempts to delete thousands of genuine voters in Aland, and serious "irregularities" in Haryana and other states, underscoring "systematic and mass manipulation" of electoral rolls. ."Instead of ordering an impartial inquiry, the Election Commission of India chose to dismiss these findings, demanded affidavits from the Leader of Opposition, and failed to share information sought by investigating agencies. ."Just months before the Bihar election, the Election Commission began the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. It has since spread to twelve states and Union Territories in its second phase, and to sixteen states and three Union Territories in its third," he said. .Venugopal claimed that the stated aim is clean rolls, but "The effect is to make citizens prove they belong." .He said Bihar's draft roll alone lost over 65 lakh names, and across the three phases deletions are now believed to exceed 13 crore. .Those most at risk are the poor, Dalits, Adivasis, minorities, migrant workers and women who moved home after marriage, the very citizens Babasaheb and Gandhiji fought to empower, the Congress leader said. .Mallikarjun Kharge targets Prime Minister Modi on price rise, says progress will not be measured by length of his speeches."All this has been possible because the Election Commission is compromised. Article 324 envisaged the ECI as an independent constitutional body, insulated from the government of the day. Yet the law was amended to remove the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for Election Commissioners, giving the government of the day a decisive say in their appointment," he said. .A further amendment extended lifetime legal immunity to Election Commissioners for acts performed in the course of their official duties, "effectively granting them a free hand to dishonour constitutional decorum and principles," he noted. ."When a citizen's vote is stolen, every other right guaranteed by the Constitution becomes meaningless. This fight is therefore not about any one party, but about whether India will remain a democracy of We, the People. ."On Constitution Day, 26 November 2026, every Pradesh Congress Committee will organise a massive Samvidhan Raksha March in its state as the centrepiece of our campaign to safeguard the Constitution," Venugopal said. .He said each march will begin at a statue of Ambedkar or Mahatma Gandhi, symbolising the Congress party's unwavering commitment to protecting the Constitution. .After paying homage to the founding fathers, Congress workers and citizens will read the Preamble aloud, recalling the values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity it upholds, and take a solemn oath to protect the Constitution, he said. .Alongside, through the Vote Rakshak campaign, Congress workers will reach every booth to verify voters whose names have been deleted and help them reclaim their right to vote. ."We appeal to every citizen who cherishes the Constitution, students and youth, farmers and workers, women, Dalit, Adivasi, OBC and minority communities, and civil society, to join these marches in large numbers and make November 26 a historic day of resolve," Venugopal said. .The Constitution gave every Indian the vote. The Indian National Congress is duty-bound and committed to defend it. Jai Hind. Jai Samvidhan," he asserted.

content: THE TRIBUNE, India’s oldest, daily English-language newspaper, was first published on February 2, 1881, in Lahore (now in Pakistan), and save for 40 days in the immediate aftermath of Partition, has come out every day over the last 145 years. THE TRIBUNE was started by Sardar Dyal Singh Majithia, a public-spirited philanthropist of the time. The newspaper is run by a five-member Trust, which is chaired by Shri N N Vohra, former Governor of J&K State (2008-2018); as well as Justice S S Sodhi, former Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court; Shri Gurbachan Jagat, former Governor of Manipur; Lt Gen. Shamsher Singh Mehta, former Western Army Commander; Shri Paramjit Singh Patwalia, Senior Advocate in the Supreme Court.THE TRIBUNE is free, objective, and independent. Restraint and moderation, rather than agitational language, are the hallmarks of the paper.The Tribune has two sister publications, Punjabi Tribune (in Punjabi) and Dainik Tribune (in Hindi).
